title: Pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis

claims.statement: In adults with alcohol dependence in double-blind outpatient trials, most of them European and most after detoxification, acamprosate compared with placebo is associated with fewer people returning to any drinking during treatment: across 16 trials pooled in a review for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, 1,968 of 2,576 people on acamprosate (76 in 100) and 1,893 of 2,271 on placebo (83 in 100) drank again (crude totals, editors' arithmetic), a pooled difference of 9 in 100 (risk difference −0.09, 95% CI −0.14 to −0.04; 12 people treated for one to benefit), with large differences between trials (I² 80.8%) (Jonas et al., 2014; funded by the agency; no conflicts declared); its 2023 update gives a risk ratio of 0.88 (0.83 to 0.93; 20 trials, 6,380 people) and a Cochrane review 0.86 (0.81 to 0.91; 24 trials) (McPheeters et al., 2023; Rösner et al., 2010). In the Cochrane review abstinent days rose by about 11 in every 100 days (10.94 percentage points, 5.08 to 16.81; I² 94%), and in 7 trials fewer people on acamprosate had returned to drinking 3 to 12 months after treatment ended (risk ratio 0.91, 0.87 to 0.96). Acamprosate did not reduce return to heavy drinking (risk ratio 0.99, 0.94 to 1.05; 7 trials). In the 4 trials at low risk of bias the difference was not clear (risk difference −0.02, −0.09 to 0.05); the two of them with by far the most events, both in the US and one of them COMBINE, found no benefit, while most of the other 15 trials were European and recruited from inpatient settings or treatment programmes. The 2014 authors list population differences, other heterogeneity, chance or 'no true association between acamprosate and return to drinking' as possible explanations. Of the Cochrane review's 24 trials, 17 were run or supported by drug companies, mostly the manufacturer, though industry-run and non-profit trials gave similar estimates (risk ratios 0.88 and 0.88). Diarrhoea was more common (11 more in 100; risk difference 0.11, 0.09 to 0.13), and more people stopped because of side effects (risk ratio 1.35, 1.01 to 1.80). Head to head, acamprosate and naltrexone did not differ (return to any drinking risk ratio 1.03, 0.96 to 1.10; 3 trials). The three reviews share most of their trials. Certainty: low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Jonas et al. 2014 (against placebo, trials at low or medium risk of bias): return to any drinking RD −0.09 (95% CI −0.14 to −0.04), 16 trials, 4847, I² 80.8%, NNT 12 (8 to 26), moderate strength of evidence; crude totals 1968/2576 (76.4%) against 1893/2271 (83.4%) (editors' arithmetic from Figure 2); by risk of bias, post hoc: high or unclear −0.13 (−0.20 to −0.06), 3 trials, 757; medium −0.11 (−0.16 to −0.06), 12 trials, 3438; low −0.02 (−0.09 to 0.05), 4 trials, 1409; return to heavy drinking −0.01 (−0.04 to 0.03), 7 trials, 2496; percentage of drinking days WMD −8.8 (−12.8 to −4.8), 13 trials; deaths 7 against 6 (8 trials, 2677), insufficient. McPheeters et al. 2023: return to any drinking RR 0.88 (0.83 to 0.93), 20 trials, 6380, moderate (I² 77.6%); return to heavy drinking 0.99 (0.94 to 1.05), 7 trials, moderate (no effect); percentage of drinking days −8.3 (−12.2 to −4.4), 14 trials; diarrhoea RR 1.58 (1.27 to 1.97). Rösner et al. 2010 (Cochrane): return to any drinking RR 0.86 (0.81 to 0.91), 24 trials, 6172, NNTB 9.09 (6.66 to 14.28); abstinent days MD 10.94 percentage points (5.08 to 16.81), 19 trials, I² 94%; after treatment RR 0.91 (0.87 to 0.96), 7 trials, 1986; return to heavy drinking 0.99 (0.94 to 1.04), 6 trials, 2132; diarrhoea RD 0.11 (0.09 to 0.13), 16 trials; drop-out because of adverse events RR 1.35 (1.01 to 1.80), 19 trials; by funding, fully industry-sponsored 0.88 (0.80 to 0.97), 11 trials, partly industry-supported 0.84 (0.78 to 0.89), 6 trials, non-profit 0.88 (0.81 to 0.96), 7 trials. COMBINE: acamprosate main effect on percent days abstinent 78.4 against 77.6 (P=.61); time to first heavy drinking day HR 0.85 (0.63 to 1.15), the paper's main-effect hazard ratio, whose basis is unclear (study card sc_anton_2006).

claims.statement: In adults with alcohol use disorder in double-blind outpatient trials of 12 to 52 weeks, mostly with a psychosocial co-intervention, other medicines compared with placebo, as pooled in a 2023 review for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (McPheeters et al., 2023; funded by the agency; no conflicts declared): topiramate is associated with fewer drinking days (−7.2 percentage points, 95% CI −14.3 to −0.1; 8 trials, 1,080 people), fewer heavy-drinking days (−6.2, −10.9 to −1.4; 9 trials) and about 2 fewer drinks on drinking days (−2.0, −3.1 to −1.0; 7 trials), each graded moderate strength of evidence by the review, with more tingling (risk ratio 3.08, 2.11 to 4.49), changes in taste (3.01, 1.70 to 5.34) and problems with thinking (2.37, 1.58 to 3.55); baclofen with fewer people returning to any drinking (risk ratio 0.83, 0.70 to 0.98; 8 trials) and gabapentin with fewer returning to heavy drinking (0.90, 0.82 to 0.98; 3 trials), both graded low, with more drowsiness, sleepiness or dizziness and, with gabapentin, problems with thinking (2.76, 1.51 to 5.06). Disulfiram did not reduce return to any drinking in blinded trials (risk ratio 1.03, 0.90 to 1.17; 3 trials; low), although no trial tested taking it under supervision, which the earlier review says may underestimate its benefit (Jonas et al., 2014). A long-acting injection of naltrexone showed no clear difference in return to any or heavy drinking (2 trials each; low). In the earlier review, nalmefene was associated with 2 fewer heavy-drinking days a month (−2.0, −3.0 to −1.0; 2 trials), and about 1 more person in 12 stopped a trial because of side effects (number needed to harm 12, 7 to 50). Deaths were too few to judge (8 with baclofen against 3 with placebo in 4 trials). The 2023 review updates the 2014 one and shares most of its trials, and it reports results only for medicines with at least low strength of evidence for benefit. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: McPheeters et al. 2023, against placebo: topiramate, percentage of drinking days WMD −7.2 (−14.3 to −0.1), 8 trials, 1080; heavy drinking days −6.2 (−10.9 to −1.4), 9 trials, 1210; drinks per drinking day −2.0 (−3.1 to −1.0), 7 trials, 922; all moderate; paraesthesia RR 3.08 (2.11 to 4.49), taste abnormalities 3.01 (1.70 to 5.34), cognitive dysfunction 2.37 (1.58 to 3.55). Baclofen, return to any drinking RR 0.83 (0.70 to 0.98), 8 trials, 995, low; drowsiness 1.46 (1.15 to 1.86), dizziness 1.89 (1.40 to 2.55), sleepiness 1.81 (1.11 to 2.97); deaths 8 against 3 (4 trials, 660), insufficient. Gabapentin, return to heavy drinking 0.90 (0.82 to 0.98), return to any drinking 0.92 (0.83 to 1.02), 3 trials, 522, low; cognitive dysfunction 2.76 (1.51 to 5.06), dizziness 1.70 (1.24 to 2.32). Disulfiram, return to any drinking 1.03 (0.90 to 1.17), 3 trials, 622, low (no effect). Injectable naltrexone, return to any drinking 0.96 (0.90 to 1.03), 2 trials, 939; return to heavy drinking 1.00 (0.82 to 1.21), 2 trials, 615; low (no effect). Jonas et al. 2014: nalmefene, heavy drinking days per month WMD −2.0 (−3.0 to −1.0), 2 trials, 806; drinks per drinking day −1.02 (−1.77 to −0.28), 3 trials, 608; withdrawal from trials because of adverse events NNH 12 (7 to 50), 5 trials, 2054.

claims.statement: In adults with alcohol dependence treated as outpatients in double-blind trials, mostly after detoxification and with counselling or another psychosocial treatment in both groups, naltrexone tablets at the dose used in most trials compared with placebo reduced return to heavy drinking (in most trials 5 or more drinks in a day for men, 4 or more for women) during 12 to 52 weeks of treatment: across 19 trials pooled in a review for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, 728 of 1,593 people on naltrexone (46 in 100) and 698 of 1,282 on placebo (54 in 100) returned to heavy drinking (crude totals, editors' arithmetic), a pooled difference of 9 in 100 (risk difference −0.09, 95% CI −0.13 to −0.04; 12 people treated for one to benefit) (Jonas et al., 2014; funded by the agency; no conflicts declared). Its 2023 update found a risk ratio of 0.81 (0.72 to 0.90; 23 trials, 3,170 people), and a Cochrane review of naltrexone in any form, mostly the same tablets, 0.83 (0.76 to 0.90; 28 trials, 4,433 people) (McPheeters et al., 2023; Rösner et al., 2010). The effect on staying off alcohol completely was small or unclear: risk difference −0.05 (−0.10 to −0.002) in 2014, risk ratio 0.93 (0.87 to 0.99) in 2023 and 0.96 (0.92 to 1.00) in the Cochrane review. People on naltrexone drank on about 5 fewer days in every 100 (−5.1 percentage points, −7.16 to −3.04) and drank heavily on about 4 fewer (−4.3, −7.60 to −0.91). Nausea (risk ratio 1.73, 1.51 to 1.98), dizziness (1.99, 1.47 to 2.69) and vomiting (1.53, 1.23 to 1.91) were more common, about 1 more person in 48 stopped a trial because of side effects (number needed to harm 48, 30 to 112), and serious adverse events were not more frequent (risk difference −0.02, −0.05 to 0.00; 9 trials). A higher oral dose and a long-acting injection were each tested in only 2 or 3 trials, without a clear effect on return to heavy drinking. Head to head, naltrexone and acamprosate did not differ (return to heavy drinking risk ratio 1.02, 0.93 to 1.11; 4 trials, more than half of the people in one US trial). Evidence on deaths, injuries and quality of life is insufficient. The three reviews share most of their trials and are one body of evidence, not three. Most participants were White men in their 40s with moderate to severe dependence who had stopped drinking before starting, and effects in people still drinking, with mild disorder or without counselling are uncertain. Certainty: moderate. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Jonas et al. 2014 (oral naltrexone, main dose group, against placebo): return to heavy drinking RD −0.09 (95% CI −0.13 to −0.04), 19 trials, 2875 participants, I² 43.7%, NNT 12 (8 to 26), moderate strength of evidence; crude totals 728/1593 (45.7%) against 698/1282 (54.4%) (editors' arithmetic from Figure 3); return to any drinking RD −0.05 (−0.10 to −0.002), 16 trials, 2347, NNT 20 (11 to 500); percentage of drinking days WMD −5.4 (−7.5 to −3.2); heavy drinking days −4.1 (−7.6 to −0.61); withdrawal from trials because of adverse events NNH 48 (30 to 112), 17 trials, 2743.
